strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in multimodal inference through a simple combination of attention-based selection and token merging, applied before the language model without changing its architecture.

PruMerge+ demonstrates a useful accuracy–compression tradeoff. At 25% token retention, the 7B model achieves 76.8 versus 78.5 on VQAv2, 57.1 versus 58.2 on TextVQA, and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench (Table 1).

Evaluation covers six image benchmarks, two language-model sizes, and three video benchmarks. Applying the method to Video-LLaVA without additional training provides encouraging transfer evidence, including improved ActivityNet-QA accuracy.

The sampling comparisons, component ablations, and visualizations provide useful supporting evidence. Table 4 shows substantial improvements over comparable spatial sampling budgets, particularly on TextVQA. The manuscript identifies and cites its underlying models, training data, and related methods.
weaknesses: Practical efficiency remains insufficiently validated. Table 2 provides roofline estimates for LLM prefill, without measured end-to-end latency, decoding performance, or pruning/merging overhead. The claimed O(n) clustering complexity also conflicts with the full key-similarity matrix in Equation 4: even restricting comparisons to m selected anchors costs O(mn), which is quadratic at a fixed retained fraction. Actual measurements are needed to establish the deployment and scalability benefits.

The comparative evaluation does not establish matched training conditions. PruMerge+ results in Table 7 match the fine-tuned results from Table 1, but equivalent adaptation for ToMe, ATS, and EViT is not specified; CrossGet numbers are imported from its paper. Because Table 6 demonstrates that fine-tuning materially improves performance, this uncertainty weakens attribution of the reported advantages to the reduction algorithm.

The central contribution of adaptive IQR selection is not isolated. A fixed top-k attention selector with the same merging procedure and matched average token budget would distinguish the benefit of adaptivity from attention ranking and merging. Threshold and neighborhood-size sensitivity, together with token-count distributions, would also strengthen the claim that the method appropriately allocates tokens according to image complexity.

Several algorithmic ambiguities hinder reproduction. Algorithm 1 doubles the selected token count for PruMerge+, which does not explain the reported 5.5% versus 25% average retention or the 50% configuration. Its merging equation omits the anchor and uses an unnormalized weighted sum, whereas the prose describes supplementing retained tokens through weighted averaging. The neighborhood size, attention-head aggregation, and LoRA hyperparameters are also unspecified. These issues need reconciliation with the evaluated implementation.

The strongest performance-preservation claims exceed the evidence. At aggressive compression, the 7B model loses 6.5 points on VQAv2, 9.6 points on POPE, and 160.4 points on MME (Table 1). Section 4.1 also claims improved POPE performance although every proposed image variant scores below its baseline. These corrections would preserve the useful fourfold-compression result, but the manuscript should clearly distinguish that result from the substantially less accurate aggressive variant.
